one_liner: Static rewriter adding ASan and AFL coverage to Linux x86-64/aarch64 binaries without source; claims 3x faster than Valgrind memcheck.
what_it_does: RetroWrite turns a compiled Linux ELF binary back into reassemblable assembly (symbolization), runs an instrumentation pass over it, and reassembles it with an ordinary compiler. Passes include binary-only AddressSanitizer (BASan, linked against the compiler's libasan), AFL coverage (on x64 by assembling the output with afl-gcc; on aarch64 through its own coverage pass plus forkserver), coarse CFI on aarch64, a jumparound obfuscation pass and a kernel-module variant (KRetrowrite, kcov). It is a Python 3 command-line tool (`retrowrite [--asan | -m <pass>] <bin> <out.s>`), not a library you link; the result is a native binary that runs without any runtime translator, unlike Valgrind.
how_it_is_fast: Instrumentation is inserted statically, so the rewritten program runs as native code with no dynamic binary translation; Valgrind memcheck instead JIT-translates every basic block at run time. On x64, relocation information in position-independent binaries tells pointers apart from constants, which lets it symbolize code and data references (including switch tables) without heuristics. The BASan pass emits the same inline shadow-memory check as compiler ASan (address >> 3, shadow offset 0x7fff8000) before each 1/2/4/8-byte access and uses a register-liveness analysis to borrow free registers and skip saving RFLAGS where possible, so checks avoid most spills. AFL coverage on x64 reuses afl-gcc's assembler instrumentation on the symbolized output, which is why it matches compiler-instrumented speed.
when_to_use: Fuzzing a closed-source Linux x86-64 PIE binary with AFL/AFL++ when QEMU mode is too slow; the paper abstract claims 4.5x over QEMU-mode AFL and parity with compiler instrumentation.
Memory-error checking of a binary-only C program where Valgrind memcheck's slowdown makes test or fuzz runs impractical (abstract: about 3x faster than memcheck on SPEC CPU2006 C benchmarks).
Stripped or non-PIE aarch64 Linux binaries, which the aarch64 rewriter supports (the x64 one does not).
Fuzzing Linux kernel modules without source via KRetrowrite with kcov or BASan.
Research or tooling that needs editable, reassemblable assembly of a binary to write a custom instrumentation pass in Python.
when_not_to_use: C++ binaries: the README marks C++ support as work in progress on both architectures, and issue #26 (g++ hello world cannot be rebuilt) is open.
Stripped or non-PIE x86-64 binaries: the x64 rewriter needs symbols and position-independent code (merging stripped-binary function detection is still open as issue #40).
When you have source: compiler AddressSanitizer is faster (the abstract snippet puts BASan about 0.65x slower than source ASan) and checks wider accesses.
When you need memcheck's uninitialized-value tracking or leak-checking semantics; BASan is an ASan-style redzone checker, so the 3x comparison is between tools that check different things.

Production or safety-critical rewriting: reassembly can silently mis-symbolize (open issues #45 RIP-relative addressing, #38 omitted data sections, #35 functions not disassembled, #49 segfaults in BASan-rewritten SPEC2006 gcc and bzip2), and the USENIX Security 2023 'Reassembly Is Hard' study (slides, search snippet only) counts RetroWrite output as compilable for 95.2% of 25,704 binaries and still reports symbolization errors; compiling is not the same as running correctly.

integration.dependencies: Python 3 (README says 3.6) with pyelftools, capstone >= 4.0.2, intervaltree and archinfo pinned to 9.1.11752; a GCC or Clang toolchain to reassemble, libasan for BASan, afl-gcc/afl-clang (AFL++) for x64 coverage
integration.min_toolchain: Python 3.6; capstone 4.0.2+ (README warns distro capstone packages may be too old)
integration.platforms: Linux ELF on x86-64 (PIE, non-stripped, non-C++ only) and aarch64 (stripped and non-PIE supported, different algorithm); no Windows or macOS
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — replaces running the binary under Valgrind memcheck (or AFL QEMU mode) with a rewrite-then-run step on supported binaries, but it reports ASan-style errors, not memcheck's, and works only on binaries the rewriter accepts

gotchas: The x64 BASan pass skips memory operands that are not 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes (it prints 'Maybe missed an access'), so 16-byte SSE/AVX accesses go unchecked, and rep stos is marked TODO.
Stack redzones are added only to functions that load a stack canary in their first 20 instructions, so binaries built without -fstack-protector get no stack-overflow detection.
Depending on the libasan version the output may fail to link with 'undefined reference to __asan_init_v4'; the README's fix is a sed rename to __asan_init.
Register analysis is slow on large binaries; the -c flag caches it next to the output, and a stale cache prints 'Missing free reglist in cache. Regenerate!' and falls back to saving registers.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick RetroWrite over Dr. Memory or Valgrind when the target is a supported Linux PIE C binary and you can afford a rewrite step, since the result runs natively with compiler-ASan-style checks; pick E9Patch when the binary is stripped, non-PIE or C++ (it patches in place with trampolines instead of reassembling), and compiler AddressSanitizer whenever you have source.
verified_claims_summary: Only the IEEE S&P 2020 abstract was readable (via search snippets): BASan about 3x faster than Valgrind memcheck and about 0.65x slower than source ASan on the SPEC CPU2006 C benchmarks, detecting 80% more bugs, and AFL coverage 4.5x faster than QEMU mode (a Purdue thesis snippet says 7.5x). CPU, compiler, flags and per-benchmark numbers are in the paper, which was unreachable (nebelwelt.net and cs.purdue.edu DNS-blocked), and the repo has no benchmark data.
